faq.q: Why does a candle need a wick?
faq.a: The wick soaks up melted wax and lifts it into the flame by capillary action, the way a paper towel soaks up a spill. Without a wick the wax would just melt into a puddle and not burn.
asks: What is the string in a candle for?

faq.q: What part of the candle actually burns?
faq.a: It is the wax vapour that burns. The heat turns the liquid wax on the wick into a gas, and that gas mixes with oxygen and burns.
asks: Is it the wick that burns?

faq.q: Why does a candle go out when you blow on it?
faq.a: Blowing pushes the flame and the wax vapour away from the wick and cools it, so there is no longer enough heat to turn wax into gas. The loop breaks and the flame dies.
asks: Why does blowing put out a candle?

faq.q: Why does the candle get shorter?
faq.a: The wax is the fuel. As it burns it joins with oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water vapour, invisible gases that drift away, so the candle gets smaller.
asks: Where does the candle wax go?

faq.q: Can you relight a candle from its smoke?
faq.a: Yes. Just after blowing it out, a lit match held in the rising white smoke can relight the wick, because that smoke is unburnt wax vapour. The flame runs down the vapour to the wick.
asks: What is the white smoke from a candle?

facts: The hottest part of a candle flame, near the tip of the faint blue zone, reaches about 1,400 degrees Celsius.
Michael Faraday gave his famous lectures The Chemical History of a Candle at the Royal Institution in London in 1848.

quiz.say: Which part of a candle actually burns?
quiz.show: Which part of a candle actually burns?
quiz.why: Heat turns liquid wax into a gas, and that wax vapour is what burns with oxygen.

wrong.1: Solid wax only melts; it has to become a gas before it can burn.
wrong.2: The wick chars a little, but its job is to carry fuel up to the flame.
